summary: Describes version 2 of S/MIME, a way to add cryptographic signatures and encryption to MIME data such as email. It was published as an informational memo, not a standard, and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to put a secret seal and a signature on your email, so only the right person can read it and they know it is really from you.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with mime
subtitle: How S/MIME version 2 wraps MIME messages in signatures and encryption using PKCS #7 objects.

tldr.problem: Ordinary MIME mail has no way to prove who sent a message, to show it was not altered, or to keep its contents private.
tldr.mechanism: S/MIME wraps a MIME entity in a PKCS #7 object that is signed, enveloped (encrypted) or both, and carries it in new MIME types such as application/pkcs7-mime and application/pkcs7-signature. Clear-signed mail uses multipart/signed.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational, not an IETF standard, and records version 2 as it was in use. It is now Historic, and its baseline 40-bit RC2 encryption is described by the RFC itself as weak.

today: RFC 2311 is marked Historic and was published as an Informational memo, not an IETF standard. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. Its own security section calls the 40-bit RC2 baseline weak.

sections.title: What S/MIME Version 2 Provides
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) adds cryptographic security to MIME data. Digital signatures give authentication, message integrity and non-repudiation of origin. Encryption gives privacy and data security.

It is not limited to mail. It works with any transport that carries MIME data, such as HTTP, and can be used by automated agents, for example to sign software-generated documents.

The RFC states plainly that it is historical material published for the public record and is not an IETF standard. Where it says "standard", it means a standard for adopters of S/MIME version 2. Requirements are split between receiving agents and sending agents, following the advice to be liberal in what you receive and conservative in what you send.
sections.plainLanguage: S/MIME lets a program put a seal on an email so you know who sent it, and lock it so only the right person can open it.

sections.title: Message Formats and MIME Types
sections.content:
The data to be secured is always a canonical MIME entity. It is handed to PKCS processing, which produces a PKCS #7 object, and that object is wrapped in MIME again. Preparation has three steps: prepare the entity locally, convert leaf parts to canonical form (text must use CR LF line endings and a named charset), and apply transfer encoding.

Three MIME types are defined:

  • application/pkcs7-mime carries one BER-encoded PKCS #7 object, either enveloped-data, signed-data or a certs-only message. Senders SHOULD add the smime-type parameter.
  • application/pkcs7-signature carries a detached signature: a signedData object with an empty content.
  • application/pkcs10 carries a PKCS #10 certification request.

Suggested file names use the extensions .p7m, .p7c, .p7s and .p10. They help across gateways, but a proper implementation MUST use the MIME types and MUST NOT rely on file extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Your message goes into a special envelope with a label saying what kind of protection it has. A file-name ending is just a hint on the outside.

sections.title: Signing, Encrypting and Both
sections.content:
There are two signed-only formats. With application/pkcs7-mime and signedData, the message is wrapped in one opaque object that only S/MIME software can read. With multipart/signed, the original entity is the first part and the signature is the second, so a recipient without S/MIME software can still read the message. Sending the multipart/signed form is generally preferred, and receivers SHOULD handle both.

A multipart/signed message has two required parameters. The protocol MUST be application/pkcs7-signature, and micalg names the digest algorithm (md5, sha1 or unknown). If it may cross 7-bit SMTP, it MUST be transfer encoded to 7-bit text, because a relay that changed or corrupted the first part would invalidate the signature.

Signing and encrypting are done by nesting the formats, and implementations MUST process arbitrarily nested S/MIME within reasonable resource limits. Signing first hides the signers inside the envelope. Enveloping first leaves signatures verifiable without a private key.

An application/pkcs7-mime object passes through a non-S/MIME gateway as an opaque attachment. This is why it survives gateways that would break a multipart/signed message.
sections.plainLanguage: You can sign a letter on the outside of the envelope so anyone can read it, or seal it so only S/MIME software can open it. You can also do both, one inside the other.

sections.title: Algorithms and Choosing Encryption
sections.content:
Receiving agents MUST support SHA-1 and MD5 digests, and sending agents SHOULD use SHA-1. RSA (rsaEncryption) is used for signatures and for encrypting the symmetric content key, with public key sizes from 512 to 1024 bits. Of the PKCS #7 content types, receivers MUST support data, signedData and envelopedData.

For content encryption, receivers MUST support RC2 with a 40-bit key (RC2/40) and SHOULD support triple DES. A signed message can carry an S/MIME capabilities attribute listing what its sender can decrypt, in order of preference, plus a signing-time attribute.

A sending agent picks encryption in order of four rules: use the recipient's known preferred capability; otherwise reuse the algorithm of the last signed and encrypted message received from them; otherwise use triple DES if it will risk failed decryption; otherwise use RC2/40. A sender that decides weak encryption is unacceptable MUST NOT use RC2/40.

Key pairs generated by an agent SHOULD be 768 to 1024 bits, and MUST NOT be under 512 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides need to know the same secret-code methods. A sender looks at what the other person said they understand and uses the best one that works.

sections.title: Weak Encryption and Its Risks
sections.content:
The RFC calls 40-bit encryption weak and says it offers little real security over plaintext. It is never recommended unless the only alternative is no cryptography. A human-controlled sending agent SHOULD let the sender weigh the risk before using RC2/40 or a similar algorithm.

It also warns against sending the same message under different strengths. An attacker watching the channel can read the strongly encrypted copy by decrypting the weakly encrypted one. Appendix C explains that the 40-bit baseline comes from US export regulations, which is why a restricted and an unrestricted profile existed.
sections.plainLanguage: A padlock that is very easy to pick is hardly better than no lock. And if you send the same letter with a strong lock and a weak lock, a snoop just opens the weak one.
